# Discussion

\[*The discussion should be about why using biomass works one place but not the other and what other mechanisms need to be included*\]

In this study we tested if community biomass is a general indicator of mechanisms mediating global change impacts on plant diversity. Our results show that this mechanism works for the temperature and nutrient limited alpine site, but less well for the sub-alpine site. At the sub-alpine site, global change affected diversity more directly than through community biomass. By including environmental affinities, specifically affinities for light and reaction, we were able to explain the underlying mechanisms of community responses to global change.

### Community biomass mediates global change impacts on diversity in alpine sites

-   Our hypothesis mostly works really well

-   Additional positive warming effect - some lower elevation species coming in? Turf colonisation is faster than extinction (cf seedclim papers)

-   Note: Biomass co-limitation by temperature and nitrogen

We expected the three global change drivers, warming, nitrogen addition, and clipping, to operate through community biomass favoring more competitive interactions, resulting in a decrease in vascular plant diversity. In line with this hypothesis, we found a strong increase in community biomass with warming and/or nitrogen addition in both alpine and sub-alpine communities, paralleling the findings of several previous studies manipulating one or both of these drivers @Humbert2016-wg, @elmendorf2012plot, @Zhang2023-xg. Warming can increase biomass because of higher rates of photosynthesis, a longer growing season, or because higher microbial activity can increase nutrient availability, while nitrogen addition directly increases nutrient availability. Our alpine site was highly temperature and nutrient limited, resulting in a four to five times increase of community biomass. This co-limitation could be the reason for the stronger mediation through biomass at the alpine site.

We found that the increase in community biomass resulted in a decrease in diversity, which has been observed in several other warming and nitrogen addition experiments @kaarlejarvi2017herbivores, @Humbert2016-wg. This could be due to a shift towards more competitive interactions, where warming and nitrogen addition favors taller and fast growing (resource-acquisitive) species such as graminoids at the expense of resource conservative species such as many forbs @Klanderud2005-yx, @Fu2016-dw, @Wang2012-cj. The negative indirect effect on diversity was mainly through shifts in species abundance (evenness) than loss of species (richness; Supplement Figure S5), suggesting an increase in abundance of species with competitive abilities rather than species loss @Humbert2016-wg, @elmendorf2012global.

While the effects of nitrogen addition and clipping were only indirectly, warming also directly increased Shannon diversity. An increase in diversity is less commonly found in warming experiments @dainese2024global, but has been shown in long-term studies @steinbauer2018accelerated. We found both an increase in species richness and evenness suggesting that both species turnover and shift in abundance were responsible for the increase in diversity.

*\[Not sure where to put the text below yet\]*

The increase in diversity only happened when no or little nitrogen was added (\< 25 kg N ha\^-1\^ y\^-1\^).\
The major change in standing biomass, diversity and evenness occurred at levels of nitrogen addition beyond 10 kg N ha^-1^ y^-1^, which is the critical load for significant changes in the structure and function of alpine and sub-alpine grasslands[(*35*)](https://paperpile.com/c/KKq9O1/4W2I).

Colonization generally happen faster than extinctions and there is often an extinction lag in alpine communities @Vandvik2020-hu, @Alexander2015-gu.

Interestingly, diversity indices based on change in abundance (i.e. evenness and diversity) showed more change in the cold alpine community in response to global change drivers, while indices based on change in species turnover (i.e. species richness and diversity), changed more in the warmer sub-alpine community. This might be because community changes in cold environments (i.e. the alpine) are often slow[(*45*)](https://paperpile.com/c/KKq9O1/ot2B) and changes in biomass (i.e. abundance) generally happen faster than species turnover (i.e. colonization or extinction) and there is often an extinction lag in alpine communities[(*14*, *15*, *46*)](https://paperpile.com/c/KKq9O1/ztDH+wbqE+5luD).

This similar relationship between the warmed alpine and ambient sub-alpine communities suggests that colder alpine plant communities are not intrinsically less productive than those at lower elevation, but are limited by temperature-related environmental factors [(*27*)](https://paperpile.com/c/KKq9O1/FMfe).

### Alternative mechanisms drive diversity shifts in the sub-alpine

**Why not biomass effect on biodiversity?**

-   Narrower range of biomass in the subalpine (less to play with).

-   Fewer species already

-   NB - note that data is more variable for diversity responses in the sub-alpine than in the alpine - other factors matter, explanatory power lower…

**Why those other non-biomass effects?**

-   Nitrogen acidification: one alternative explanation for the non-biomass negative effect of nitrogen is soil acidification. shown by Ellenberg pH trait distribution to be shifting towards lower pH optima and especially loss of the higher-pH part of the community in the higher N treatments.

-   Drought: one explanation for the non-biomass negative effect of warming in the sub-alpine could be drought. However, we see more an increase in moisture for warmer sub-alpine communities.

-   Note: Biomass additive / compensatory effects of nitrogen and warming.

The drop in biomass at high levels of nitrogen addition could result from soil acidification[(*40*)](https://paperpile.com/c/KKq9O1/oG7A). In our study, this is supported by an increase in available calcium at high levels of nitrogen addition, which can be released from the bedrock under acid conditions (Figure S5, Table S5).

The biomass of the warmed sub-alpine community did not increase above the maximum levels found at ambient climate, but reached the same biomass across the whole nitrogen gradient, indicating growth limited by other factors, possibly lower water availability at the warmer site[(*41*)](https://paperpile.com/c/KKq9O1/nJXV), which might have been especially prominent due to a dry growing season in 2022 ( Figure S1).

### *\[Weak grazing effects\]*

-   Why so weak grazing effects?? Treatment levels? Time? Grazing only + for diversity when (i) other drivers are having negative effects and (ii) the additional species are available for colonisation and (iii) there is enough time….

**Some interesting points (unclear how to use these):**

-   The net effects of warming and nitrogen on traits encapsulates both non-biomass and biomass effects, and so should generally be less clear in terms of height.

-   Note that the warmed alpine and the unwarmed subalpine have very similar N slopes. They are living in the same climate! So even if the community is different, the N limitation is real at this temperature, but not colder (or warmer)

### Conclusions, implications

-   Several drivers work through same mechanisms, BUT at the same time, one driver can operate through several mechanisms at the same time….

-   This varies across sites (as in, the relative importance of drivers, processes) -\> asks for replicated experiments

-   Understanding how drivers map onto processes - we need to understand processes, find proxies, etc. We find that traits can help understand processes, and we might need to find ecosystem or community (Ellenberg, trait) proxies for these.

-   Ellenbergs are useful! Proxies for envt response. Map them onto other traits?
